content.text: A key tells React which data item an element stands for, so the item's state and DOM can follow it when the list changes. An array index names a position, not an item: when items are inserted, removed or reordered, state stays at the old position and ends up on the wrong item. Use a stable id from your data.

A bug report from the mail team: "I opened an email from Sara. A new email arrived, and now Sara's email is collapsed and the new one is open." Nobody touched the expand logic in months. The list renders with
, added years ago to silence a console warning, and that one attribute is the whole bug.

The belief: keys are a React formality. The console complains when a list has none, any unique value makes the complaint go away, and the array index is unique and always available, so it's the obvious choice.

It's easy to see why it sticks. The warning is the only feedback most people get about keys, so fixing the warning feels like the goal. Index keys also work perfectly in the demo: a static list renders fine, and nothing breaks until an item is added at the top, deleted or sorted. And unique among siblings is a real rule. It's just not the only one: a key also has to keep naming the same item from one render to the next.

When a list re-renders, React has to pair each new child with one from the previous render. That pairing decides what survives: a matched component keeps its state and its DOM nodes and just receives new props, while an unmatched one is created from scratch. This matching is part of
is what it matches on. React's docs compare keys to file names in a folder: without names, you'd refer to files by their order, and deleting one would quietly renumber all the rest.
An index key matches by position
If you don't pass a key at all, React uses the index. So

silences the warning and changes nothing else: React still matches "the child at position 0" with "the child at position 0". As long as items never move, position and identity are the same thing. The moment they diverge, state goes with the position:

content.text: Walk through the bug. Sara's email is first, so its row has key
. A new email arrives at the top. On the next render, key
belongs to the new email, so React reuses the existing component at key
, keeps its state, and passes it the new email as a prop. The new email shows up open. Sara's email moves to key
, which used to be the second row's component, with
. Nothing was lost or created at random; every piece of state stayed exactly at its position. With
, React sees that Sara's key moved to the second place, moves her component there, and creates a fresh, closed row for the newcomer.
The same thing happens to anything a row holds that doesn't come from props: text typed into an uncontrolled
, focus, a checked box, a playing animation. Props get updated; everything else sticks to the key.
silences the warning too, but the keys never match between renders. React recreates every row and its DOM on every render, which is slow and wipes whatever the user typed.
Data from a database already has ids. Data you create in the browser, like a draft note or a new form row, should get an id once, at the moment it's created, and keep it for life:
Keys only need to be unique among siblings, not across the app, and your component never receives
as a prop. If it needs the id, pass it separately:

What about content as a key, like the subject line? It holds only while the content is unique and never edited. Two emails titled "Invoice" collide, and editing a note whose text is its key gives it a new key, so React resets that row.

Open a row, type into an input, then add an item at the top or sort the list. If the open row or the text moves to a different item, a key is naming a position.

items.text: A key names an item, not a slot: it's how React decides which state and DOM belong to which data.
An index key is exactly what React does without a key; it silences the warning and nothing more.
When items move, index-keyed state stays at its position and shows up on the wrong item.
Use stable ids from your data, create ids for local items once, and never generate keys during render.
